# Detailed chronological account: MiniMax-M2.7 on `C1_task_089` (P1, Explicit-Transient)

## Source material consulted
- The task spec and ground-truth perturbed trace: `/opt/dlami/nvme/tmp/ToolMaze-hf/perturbed_tasks/c1/C1_task_089_P1.json` (and the un-perturbed base `tasks/c1/C1_task_089.json`).
- The ToolMaze paper's Appendix E case-study caption (`sections/Appendix.tex`, `tables/case_study.tex`).
- The Figure 7 case-study PDF: `figs/case_study/case_study_C1_task_089_P1.pdf`, which shows the two side-by-side execution traces (Claude-Sonnet-4.6 succeeds, MiniMax-M2.7 fails).
- The failure-aware system prompt actually used for P1 runs (`tables/evaluation_prompts1.tex`).

## The task that was given

The natural-language query (Shopping/General domain, complexity C1, linear DAG):

> "Hi, for user_123, please reserve 1 black Sony XM5 for me using product_id p_sony_xm5_blk. The title is Untitled and the data is test. After you place the hold, please prepare the checkout from that reservation and let me know exactly when the reservation expires. Then suggest some popular alternatives in the same category, and send me an in-app notification with all the details."

The ground-truth single-path DAG (5 sub-tasks):

1. `hold_inventory` (Source/Action)
2. `build_checkout_from_hold` (Processor)
3. `convert_datetime` (Processor) — **the victim tool**
4. `get_recommendations_popularity` (Source)
5. `create_document_and_alert_from_data` (Action)

The agent ran under the failure-aware system prompt (the P1–P4 prompt in `evaluation_prompts1.tex`), which states: "Tools may occasionally fail or return unexpected data," "you must complete ALL [sub-tasks] — do NOT skip any sub-tasks," "Every fact … must come from a tool call," and "If you determine that a required step cannot be accomplished by any available tool or approach, stop the workflow and clearly report which step failed and why."

## The injected perturbation

The Perturbation Engine was configured with a P1 (Explicit-Transient) fault on `convert_datetime` at perturbation_point = 2 (i.e., the third tool call in the DAG). On the **first** call to `convert_datetime(timestamp=1710000300)` the engine returns:

```
{"error": "Internal Server Error"}   status: 500 InternalServerError
```

A **second** call to the same tool with the same arguments would have returned the clean payload `{"original_timestamp": 1710000300, "formatted_time": "2024-03-09 16:05"}` — i.e., the fault is transient and recovers on retry.

## What MiniMax-M2.7 actually did (chronological, from Fig. 7)

Step 1. Called `hold_inventory(product_id="p_sony_xm5_blk", user_id="user_123", quantity=1)`. The simulator returned the reservation payload (reservation_id `RESV-14729548`, `expiry_time 1710000300`, etc.). Status: success.

Step 2. Called `build_checkout_from_hold(hold_data=…, quantity=1)`, passing through the full hold payload. The simulator returned `{reservation_id, product_id, quantity}`. Status: success.

Step 3. Called `convert_datetime(timestamp=1710000300)` once. The Perturbation Engine returned the injected explicit error `{"error": "Internal Server Error"}` with HTTP-500 `InternalServerError`. This is the "! P1" event marked in Figure 7.

Step 4. **The agent did not call `convert_datetime` again.** Instead of retrying the failed processor (which would have succeeded on the second invocation per the P1 semantics), it moved on and called `get_recommendations_popularity(product_id="p_sony_xm5_blk", user_id="user_123")`. The simulator returned the two recommended alternatives (`p_sony_xm5_slv`, `p_apple_airpods`). Status: success.

Step 5. Called `create_document_and_alert_from_data(title="Untitled", data="test", user_id="user_123", priority="medium", channel="app")`. The simulator returned a `Notification sent successfully` payload. Status: success.

Step 6. The agent produced a final answer to the user and stopped.

## Signals the agent had received

- An explicit, machine-readable HTTP 500 / `InternalServerError` body on the `convert_datetime` call — exactly the kind of "explicit failure" the failure-aware prompt warns about.
- A system prompt that explicitly instructs the agent that tools "may occasionally fail" and that requires either completion of all sub-tasks or an explicit aborted-with-reason halt; it does not authorize silently skipping a sub-task.
- A standing user requirement to "let me know exactly when the reservation expires" — the very piece of information the failed `convert_datetime` call was needed to produce.

## Where things went wrong

After the single 500 response from `convert_datetime`, the agent:
- did not retry the same tool with the same arguments (the canonical recovery for transient faults under P1),
- did not halt and report the failure with a reason (the alternative authorized by the failure-aware prompt),
- did not surface the missing expiry time to the user.

Instead it skipped over the victim node entirely and proceeded to the two downstream tools, then concluded.

## Final outcome

ToolMaze's grader marked the trajectory FAIL with the explicit diagnostic shown in Figure 7:

> "P1 failed: no retry on 'convert_datetime' (called 1 time(s), need >=2); 'convert_datetime' never succeeded after retries; missing required tools: ['convert_datetime']"

The companion model in the same figure (`claude-sonnet-4-6`) called `convert_datetime` a second time after the 500, received the clean `formatted_time` payload, completed the remaining two tools, and PASSED — confirming the transient fault was recoverable by a single retry.

1	\section{The \ourmethod Framework}
2	\label{sec:framework}
3	
4	\ourmethod evaluates LLM agents along two orthogonal axes --- \emph{task complexity} ($\mathcal C$) and \emph{perturbation mode} ($\mathcal P$) --- whose cross product defines a structured evaluation space. As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:overview}, the framework is implemented as a pipeline consisting of task construction, perturbation engine, and evaluation.
5	
6	\subsection{Tool Corpus}
7	\label{sec:corpus}
8	
9	\ourmethod ships with a curated tool corpus of 270 tools, manually constructed based on real-world APIs and annotated with two complementary metadata attributes:
10	
11	\noindent\textbf{Functional category.}
12	We distinguish three functional categories.
13	Source tools retrieve information from the simulated environment, for example \texttt{get\_weather} or \texttt{search\_news}.
14	Processor tools transform intermediate data with representative examples including \texttt{temperature\_converter} and \texttt{text\_translator}.
15	Action tools represent operations with external side effects and typically serve as terminal nodes, for example \texttt{send\_email} or \texttt{book\_flight}.
16	This three-way taxonomy imposes structural constraints during DAG construction. A well-formed task DAG must contain at least one Source node and one Action node, with Processor nodes and optional Action nodes bridging the two.
17	
18	\noindent\textbf{Application domain.}
19	Tools are labeled with one of six domains: Financial, Travel, Office, Shopping, IoT, and General, covering a broad spectrum of realistic LLM tool-use scenarios from enterprise workflows to smart-home automation.
20	Domain labels constrain sampling during DAG construction to ensure semantic coherence. For example, a Travel-domain task will not chain a stock-price lookup with an email-sending action.
21	The framework further applies domain-balanced sampling so that generated tasks are distributed evenly across all six domains, preventin

# Detailed chronological account: MiniMax-M2.7 on `C1_task_089` (P1, Explicit-Transient)

## Source material consulted
- The task spec and ground-truth perturbed trace: `/opt/dlami/nvme/tmp/ToolMaze-hf/perturbed_tasks/c1/C1_task_089_P1.json` (and the un-perturbed base `tasks/c1/C1_task_089.json`).
- The ToolMaze paper's Appendix E case-study caption (`sections/Appendix.tex`, `tables/case_study.tex`).
- The Figure 7 case-study PDF: `figs/case_study/case_study_C1_task_089_P1.pdf`, which shows the two side-by-side execution traces (Claude-Sonnet-4.6 succeeds, MiniMax-M2.7 fails).
- The failure-aware system prompt actually used for P1 runs (`tables/evaluation_prompts1.tex`).

## The task that was given

The natural-language query (Shopping/General domain, complexity C1, linear DAG):

> "Hi, for user_123, please reserve 1 black Sony XM5 for me using product_id p_sony_xm5_blk. The title is Untitled and the data is test. After you place the hold, please prepare the checkout from that reservation and let me know exactly when the reservation expires. Then suggest some popular alternatives in the same category, and send me an in-app notification with all the details."

The ground-truth single-path DAG (5 sub-tasks):

1. `hold_inventory` (Source/Action)
2. `build_checkout_from_hold` (Processor)
3. `convert_datetime` (Processor) — **the victim tool**
4. `get_recommendations_popularity` (Source)
5. `create_document_and_alert_from_data` (Action)

The agent ran under the failure-aware system prompt (the P1–P4 prompt in `evaluation_prompts1.tex`), which states: "Tools may occasionally fail or return unexpected data," "you must complete ALL [sub-tasks] — do NOT skip any sub-tasks," "Every fact … must come from a tool call," and "If you determine that a required step cannot be accomplished by any available tool or approach, stop the workflow and clearly report which step failed and why."

## The injected perturbation

The Perturbation Engine was configured with a P1 (Explicit-Transient) fault on `convert_datetime` at perturbation_point = 2 (i.e., the third tool call in the DAG). On the **first** call to `convert_datetime(timestamp=1710000300)` the engine returns:

```
{"error": "Internal Server Error"}   status: 500 InternalServerError
```

A **second** call to the same tool with the same arguments would have returned the clean payload `{"original_timestamp": 1710000300, "formatted_time": "2024-03-09 16:05"}` — i.e., the fault is transient and recovers on retry.

## What MiniMax-M2.7 actually did (chronological, from Fig. 7)

Step 1. Called `hold_inventory(product_id="p_sony_xm5_blk", user_id="user_123", quantity=1)`. The simulator returned the reservation payload (reservation_id `RESV-14729548`, `expiry_time 1710000300`, etc.). Status: success.

Step 2. Called `build_checkout_from_hold(hold_data=…, quantity=1)`, passing through the full hold payload. The simulator returned `{reservation_id, product_id, quantity}`. Status: success.

Step 3. Called `convert_datetime(timestamp=1710000300)` once. The Perturbation Engine returned the injected explicit error `{"error": "Internal Server Error"}` with HTTP-500 `InternalServerError`. This is the "! P1" event marked in Figure 7.

Step 4. **The agent did not call `convert_datetime` again.** Instead of retrying the failed processor (which would have succeeded on the second invocation per the P1 semantics), it moved on and called `get_recommendations_popularity(product_id="p_sony_xm5_blk", user_id="user_123")`. The simulator returned the two recommended alternatives (`p_sony_xm5_slv`, `p_apple_airpods`). Status: success.

Step 5. Called `create_document_and_alert_from_data(title="Untitled", data="test", user_id="user_123", priority="medium", channel="app")`. The simulator returned a `Notification sent successfully` payload. Status: success.

Step 6. The agent produced a final answer to the user and stopped.

## Signals the agent had received

- An explicit, machine-readable HTTP 500 / `InternalServerError`

Despite a failure-aware system prompt warning that 'tools may occasionally fail' and requiring either full completion or an explicit halt, the agent neither retried the failed processor nor aborted with a reason; it silently skipped the victim node and proceeded to get_recommendations_popularity and create_document_and_alert_from_data.
